questions.problem:
Which of the following functions are piecewise continuous on $x\in [0,\pi ].$

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}x-1,\, & x\ne 1 \\ 2,\, & x=1,\end{aligned}\,g(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,h(x)={2}^{x+1}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A function $f(x)$ is piecewise continuous on $x\in [a,b]$ if

- it is continuous on $[a,b]$ except at finitely many points, and

- at each point of discontinuity, the one-sided limits exist and are finite.

In other words, there can only be finitely many discontinuities, and each of them must be either a point or a jump discontinuity.

With that in mind, let's examine each function.

- The function $f(x)$ is piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,\pi ]$ since it is continuous over $x\in [0,\pi ]$ except at the point $x=1,$ where the one-sided limits exist and are finite:

$$
{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x)=0
$$

- The function $g(x)$ is not piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,\pi ]$ since the one-sided limits at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ are infinite:

$$
{lim}_{x\to \pi /{2}^{-}}g(x)=+\infty ,\,{lim}_{x\to \pi /{2}^{+}}g(x)=-\infty 
$$

- The function $h(x)$ is piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,\pi ]$ since it is continuous over $x\in [0,\pi ].$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$f$ and $h$ only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following functions are piecewise continuous on $x\in [-5,\infty ).$

$$
f(x)=⌈x⌉,\,g(x)=u(x+1)+u(x+4),\,h(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x
$$

Note that $u(x)$ is the unit step function, and $⌈x⌉$ is the ceiling function.
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $I⊆R.$ A function $f:I\to R$ is piecewise continuous on $I$ if it is piecewise continuous on every closed and bounded subinterval $[a,b]⊂I.$

With that in mind, let's examine each function.

- The function $f(x)$ is piecewise continuous over $x\in [-5,\infty ).$ The function has jump discontinuities at $x=…,-2,-1,0,1,2,…,$ and any closed interval $[a,b]⊂[-5,\infty )$ will contain finitely many discontinuities.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14042449/assets/788b349598dcabebf92609183b3c48851d75bb11e22efff881a208e58be510b9.png)

- The function $g(x)$ is piecewise continuous over $x\in [-5,\infty )$ since it is continuous over $x\in [-5,\infty )$ except at the points $x=-4$ and $x=-1,$ where the one-sided limits exist and are finite:

$$
{lim}_{x\to -{4}^{-}}g(x)=0,\,{lim}_{x\to -{4}^{+}}g(x)=1
$$

$$
{lim}_{x\to -{1}^{-}}g(x)=1,\,{lim}_{x\to -{1}^{+}}g(x)=2
$$

- The function $h(x)$ is not piecewise continuous over $x\in [-5,\infty ).$ Consider the closed subinterval $x\in [0,\pi ].$ Notice that the one-sided limits at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ are infinite:

$$
{lim}_{x\to \pi /{2}^{-}}h(x)=+\infty ,\,{lim}_{x\to \pi /{2}^{+}}h(x)=-\infty .
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$f$ and $g$ only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following functions are piecewise smooth on $x\in [-1,1]?$

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}2x-\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}, & x<0 \\ x+\sqrt[5]{{x}^{2}}, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}\,,\,g(x)=4x-\sqrt[7]{{x}^{3}},\,h(x)=3{x}^{2}+\sqrt[5]{{x}^{3}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A function $f(x)$ is **piecewise smooth** on $x\in [a,b]$ if

- $f(x)$ is piecewise continuous on $[a,b],$ and

- ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists and is continuous except possibly at finitely many points, where its one-sided limits exist and are finite.

With that in mind, let's examine each function.

- The function $f(x)$ is not piecewise smooth on $x\in [-1,1].$ We split the interval at $x=0.$ On the open intervals $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1),$ we have

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}2x-{x}^{2/3}, & x<0 \\ x+{x}^{2/5}, & x>0\end{aligned}\,,
$$

so

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={\begin{aligned}2-\frac{2}{3{x}^{1/3}}, & x<0 \\ 1+\frac{2}{5{x}^{3/5}}, & x>0\end{aligned}
$$

While this derivative is continuous on the open pieces $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1),$ the limits of the derivative as $x\to 0$ are not finite. In fact, the derivative becomes unbounded near $x=0.$ Thus, the condition for finite limits at the endpoints is not met.

- The function $g(x)=4x-\sqrt[7]{{x}^{3}}$ is not piecewise smooth on $x\in [-1,1].$ We split the interval at $x=0$ into the two open intervals $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1).$ For $x\ne 0,$

$$
g(x)=4x-{x}^{3/7},
$$

so

$$
{g}^{′}(x)=4-\frac{3}{7{x}^{4/7}}.
$$

While this derivative is continuous on the open pieces $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1),$ the limits of the derivative as $x\to 0$ are not finite. In fact, the derivative becomes unbounded near $x=0.$ Thus, the condition for finite limits at the endpoints is not met.

- The function $h(x)=3{x}^{2}+\sqrt[5]{{x}^{3}}$ is not piecewise smooth on $x\in [-1,1].$ We split the interval at $x=0$ into the two open intervals $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1).$ For $x\ne 0,$

$$
h(x)=3{x}^{2}+{x}^{3/5},
$$

so

$$
{h}^{′}(x)=6x+\frac{3}{5{x}^{2/5}}.
$$

While this derivative is continuous on the open pieces $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1),$ the limits of the derivative as $x\to 0$ are not finite. In fact, the derivative becomes unbounded near $x=0.$ Thus, the condition for finite limits at the endpoints is not met.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the functions."

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}3x-1, & x<\frac{1}{2} \\ 3x+2, & x>\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}\,,
$$

so

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={\begin{aligned}3, & x<\frac{1}{2} \\ 3, & x>\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $f(x)$ and ${f}^{′}(x)$ are piecewise continuous on each open interval, and they both have finite limits at the endpoints of the subintervals.

- The function $g(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{x})$ is not piecewise smooth on $x\in [0,1].$ For $x\in (0,1),$

$$
{g}^{′}(x)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{x})}{2\sqrt{x}}.
$$

While this derivative is continuous on the open piece $(0,1),$ the limit of the derivative as $x\to {0}^{+}$ is not finite. In fact, the derivative becomes unbounded near $x=0.$ Thus, the condition for finite limits at the endpoints is not met.

- The function $h(x)=\sqrt[4]{x}$ is not piecewise smooth on $x\in [0,1].$ For $x\in (0,1),$

$$
h(x)={x}^{1/4},
$$

so

$$
{h}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{4{x}^{3/4}}.
$$

While this derivative is continuous on the open piece $(0,1),$ the limit of the derivative as $x\to {0}^{+}$ is not finite. In fact, the derivative becomes unbounded near $x=0.$ Thus, the condition for finite limits at the endpoints is not met.

$$
f(x)={x}^{3/5},
$$

so

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{3}{5{x}^{2/5}}.
$$

While this derivative is continuous on the open pieces $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1),$ the limits of the derivative as $x\to 0$ are not finite. In fact, the derivative becomes unbounded near $x=0.$ Thus, the condition for finite limits at the endpoints is not met.

$$

$$

Here, $g(x)$ and ${g}^{′}(x)$ are continuous on each open interval, but the limit of ${g}^{′}(x)$ as $x\to {0}^{+}$ is not finite because $\frac{3}{7{x}^{4/7}}$ becomes unbounded. Thus, the condition for finite limits at the endpoints is not met.

- The function $h(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}})$ is not piecewise smooth on $x\in [-1,1].$ We split the interval at $x=0$ into the two open intervals $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1).$ For $x\ne 0,$

$$

$$

so

questions.worked_solution:
A function $f(x)$ is **piecewise smooth** on $x\in [a,b]$ if

- $f(x)$ is piecewise continuous on $[a,b],$ and

- ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists and is continuous except possibly at finitely many points, where its one-sided limits exist and are finite.

With that in mind, let's examine each function.

- The function $f(x)=2x+\sqrt[5]{{x}^{2}}$ is not piecewise smooth on $x\in [-1,1].$ We split the interval at $x=0$ into the two open intervals $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1).$ For $x\ne 0,$

$$
f(x)=2x+{x}^{2/5},
$$

so

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=2+\frac{2}{5{x}^{3/5}}.
$$

While this derivative is continuous on the open pieces $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1),$ the limits of the derivative as $x\to 0$ are not finite. In fact, the derivative becomes unbounded near $x=0.$ Thus, the condition for finite limits at the endpoints is not met.

- The function $g(x)$ is piecewise smooth on $x\in [-1,1].$ We split the interval at $x=0.$ On each open interval, $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1),$ the function is linear. On these intervals,

$$
g(x)={\begin{aligned}-4x+1, & x<0 \\ -4x+3, & x>0\end{aligned}\,,
$$

so

$$
{g}^{′}(x)={\begin{aligned}-4, & x<0 \\ -4, & x>0\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $g(x)$ and ${g}^{′}(x)$ are piecewise continuous on each open interval, and they both have finite limits at the endpoints of the subintervals.

- The function $h(x)=x\sqrt[5]{x}$ is piecewise smooth on $x\in [-1,1].$ Since

$$
h(x)={x}^{6/5},
$$

we have

$$
{h}^{′}(x)=\frac{6}{5}{x}^{1/5}.
$$

Here, $h(x)$ and ${h}^{′}(x)$ are continuous on $[-1,1].$ Thus, $h(x)$ is continuously differentiable on the whole interval, and hence piecewise smooth.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$g$ and $h$ only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following functions are piecewise smooth on $x\in [-1,1]?$

$$
f(x)={x}^{2}\sqrt[7]{{x}^{2}},\,g(x)={x}^{3}+\sqrt[5]{{x}^{8}},\,h(x)={\begin{aligned}5x-3, & x<0 \\ 5x+4, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A function $f(x)$ is **piecewise smooth** on $x\in [a,b]$ if

- $f(x)$ is piecewise continuous on $[a,b],$ and

- ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists and is continuous except possibly at finitely many points, where its one-sided limits exist and are finite.

With that in mind, let's examine each function.

- The function $f(x)={x}^{2}\sqrt[7]{{x}^{2}}$ is piecewise smooth on $x\in [-1,1].$ Since

$$
f(x)={x}^{2}\sqrt[7]{{x}^{2}}={x}^{16/7},
$$

we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{16}{7}{x}^{9/7}.
$$

Here, $f(x)$ and ${f}^{′}(x)$ are continuous on $[-1,1].$ Thus, $f(x)$ is continuously differentiable on the whole interval, and hence piecewise smooth.

- The function $g(x)={x}^{3}+\sqrt[5]{{x}^{8}}$ is piecewise smooth on $x\in [-1,1].$ Since

$$
g(x)={x}^{3}+{x}^{8/5},
$$

we have

$$
{g}^{′}(x)=3{x}^{2}+\frac{8}{5}{x}^{3/5}.
$$

Here, $g(x)$ and ${g}^{′}(x)$ are continuous on $[-1,1].$ Thus, $g(x)$ is continuously differentiable on the whole interval, and hence piecewise smooth.

- The function $h(x)$ is piecewise smooth on $x\in [-1,1].$ We split the interval at $x=0.$ On each open interval, $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1),$ the function is linear. On these intervals,

$$
h(x)={\begin{aligned}5x-3, & x<0 \\ 5x+4, & x>0\end{aligned}\,,
$$

so

$$
{h}^{′}(x)={\begin{aligned}5, & x<0 \\ 5, & x>0\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $h(x)$ and ${h}^{′}(x)$ are piecewise continuous on each open interval, and they both have finite limits at the endpoints of the subintervals.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$f,$ $g,$ and $h.$"

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Piecewise-Continuous Functions Over Closed Intervals
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following functions are piecewise continuous on $x\in [0,\pi].$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14042449/assets/93b55a42a534e4f547b1cab1b700d96b4d5b51656f2090673eb051fefe44221d.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A function $f(x)$ is piecewise continuous on $x\in [a,b]$ if

- it is continuous on $[a,b]$ except at finitely many points, and

- at each point of discontinuity, the one-sided limits exist and are finite.

In other words, there can only be finitely many discontinuities, and each of them must be either a point or a jump discontinuity.

With that in mind, let's examine each function.

- The function $f(x)$ is not piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,\pi]$ since the one-sided limits at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ are infinite:

$$
\lim\limits_{x\to\pi/2^-}f(x) = +\infty, \qquad \lim\limits_{x\to\pi/2^+}f(x) = -\infty
$$

- The function $g(x)$ is piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,\pi]$ since it is continuous over $x\in [0,\pi].$

- The function $h(x)$ is piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,\pi]$ since it is continuous over $x\in [0,\pi]$ except at the point $x=1,$ where the one-sided limits exist and are finite:

$$
\lim\limits_{x\to1^-}h(x) = 3, \qquad \lim\limits_{x\to1^+}h(x) = 4
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$g$ and $h$ only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Piecewise-Continuous Functions Over Infinite Intervals
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following functions are piecewise continuous on $x\in [0,\infty).$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={\begin{aligned}1,\, & ⌈x⌉\text{ is even} \\ -1,\, & ⌈x⌉\text{ is odd}\end{aligned} \\ g(x) & =u(x-1)+u\,(x-\frac{1}{2})+u\,(x-\frac{1}{3})+⋯ \\ h(x) & =⌈\frac{x}{2}⌉\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $u(x)$ is the unit step function, and $\lceil x \rceil$ is the ceiling function.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Suppose $I\subseteq \mathbb R.$ A function $f: I \to \mathbb R$ is piecewise continuous on $I$ if it is piecewise continuous on every closed and bounded subinterval $[a,b]\subset I.$

With that in mind, let's examine each function.

- The function $f(x)$ is piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,\infty).$ The function has jump discontinuities at $x=1,2,3,\ldots,$ and any closed interval $[a,b]\subset [0,\infty)$ will contain finitely many discontinuities.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14042449/assets/3ce7aa18de332c3eb1bc57b6bf7c50acf1573717d642c731a18a85f4f9fb813a.png)

- The function $g(x)$ is not piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,\infty).$ Consider the closed subinterval $x\in [0,1].$ Notice that the function has jump discontinuities at $x=1,\dfrac12,\dfrac13,\dfrac14,\ldots,$ so it has infinitely many discontinuities on this closed interval.

- The function $h(x)$ is piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,\infty).$ The function has jump discontinuities at $x=0,2,4,\ldots,$ and any closed interval $[a,b]\subset [0,\infty)$ will contain finitely many discontinuities.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14042449/assets/9a5cc55dc36927437d16d09b4e491305efebac9d9a8995a741d62b6395a101bd.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "$f$ and $h$ only."
